extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and discretionary rules courts apply when deciding whether to grant, continue, dissolve, or refuse injunctions in patent infringement litigation (interlocutory and at final hearing). Covers notice, affidavits, evidentiary weight (possession/use/recoveries), balancing hardships, and when to send patentee to law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice requirement for injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: In the courts of the United States, notice that an injunction is to be applied for must be served on the defendant; no injunction, temporary or final, can be granted without reasonable previous notice to the adverse party or his attorneys of the time and place of moving for the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Injunctions in patent cases are not granted ex parte; reasonable prior notice of the motion must be given. (See §323.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of original inventorship when moving early
rubrics_metrics.description: It is usual, on moving for an injunction before the answer has been filed, to read an affidavit that the plaintiff believes himself to be the original and first inventor of the thing patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a special affidavit may be required where circumstances may subsequently have arisen that put the patentee's originality in doubt; courts (e.g., Justice Washington) have required and read such affidavits in support of the bill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent plus exclusive possession of some duration supports injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patent has been granted and there has been an exclusive possession of some duration under it, the court will interpose its injunction without putting the party previously to establish the validity of his patent by an action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lord Eldon's rule adopted by US courts: issuance of the patent combined with evidence of use/possession for some time creates a prima facie right to injunctive relief absent strong opposing proof. The fact of enjoyment/possession strengthens the presumption of validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: New ('patent of yesterday') patents may be sent to law first
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the patent is 'but of yesterday', and it is urged that there is no good specification or other reason the patent ought not to have been granted, the court will not act on its own notions but will send the patentee to law to establish validity before granting an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent is recent or the record shows obvious/speculative defects, the court will require a prior legal determination rather than granting interlocutory equity relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bill must state a clear right and be verified to obtain injunction on filing
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice is to grant an injunction upon the filing of the bill, and before a trial at law, if the bill states a clear right and verifies the same by affidavit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A verified bill that alleges exclusive possession, use, or sale under the patent can justify an injunction even when some doubts exist as to validity, provided the bill makes out a clear prima facie case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glaring defects in patent/specification defeat interlocutory injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: If the defects in the patent or specification are so glaring that the court can entertain no doubt as to that point, it would be unjust to restrain the defendant and the plaintiff will be required to try his title at law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts refuse interlocutory injunctions where the patent contains obvious, gross defects making its validity unsustainable on preliminary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional evidence required beyond mere issue of patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides the mere issue of the patent, additional evidence is required: that after procuring the patent the plaintiff proceeded to put that right into exercise or use for some time without being disturbed. This strengthens the probability that the patent is good and alone often justifies an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of supplementary evidence: public sales, repeated use, long enjoyment, and prior recoveries against infringers. Mere grant of letters-patent (without use/possession) is usually insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recoveries against others strengthen presumption of validity
rubrics_metrics.description: That the patentee has successfully prosecuted other persons for violating the patent (recoveries) furnishes strong public assurance that the patent is a good one and supports issuance/continuance of an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior judgments (if not collusive) and long undisturbed use together create a strong color of title that is not lightly displaced by mere affidavits to the contrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three procedural classes and differing standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases are to be considered in three classes: (1) where nothing before the court but the bill and affidavits; (2) where injunction is asked for before final hearing but respondent offers evidence affecting validity; (3) where question comes on at the hearing with full proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards and required proof vary by stage: (1) prima facie showing may suffice; (2) court weighs opposing affidavits and the strength of possession/use; (3) at final hearing a fuller inquiry is required and plaintiff is expected to have pursued legal remedies earlier if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing factors when opposing evidence is adduced
rubrics_metrics.description: When the injunction is asked before the hearing but opposing evidence is adduced, the court weighs: how far and for what length of time there has been exclusive possession; how far the respondent has raised doubts as to novelty, patentability, or infringement; and how far long possession will counteract evidence impeaching validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court exercises discretion by balancing these elements to decide whether the patentee's prima facie right has been answered and whether a trial at law is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie right: patent + long possession + infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: There is prima facie right to an injunction, without a trial at law, upon certain things being shown, namely, a patent, long possession, and infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If these are shown and not displaced by respondent's evidence, the injunction should issue; the inquiry is whether respondent's evidence sufficiently answers that prima facie right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavits casting doubt do not outweigh strong possession/recoveries
rubrics_metrics.description: When the presumption in favor of validity has been strengthened by long enjoyment and recoveries, it will not be sufficient for the defendant to read affidavits tending to cast doubts on originality, especially if that evidence is answered by stronger evidence from the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In preliminary proceedings where there is no cross-examination, it is unsafe to decide against validity when the patentee's enjoyments/recitals create strong presumption; courts favor preserving the status quo until full trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicting evidence on possession/novelty requires trial
rubrics_metrics.description: If the respondent succeeds in raising doubts both as to exclusive possession and as to the novelty of what is claimed, and the evidence on these points is conflicting, the injunction will be refused until a trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the preliminary evidence is in conflict such that the prima facie right is displaced, the proper remedy is a trial at law rather than interlocutory equity relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubtful infringement must be tried by jury
rubrics_metrics.description: If the question of infringement is doubtful it must be tried by a jury; courts have dissolved injunctions and ordered an action to try the infringement, often with an order that defendants keep an account and admit the plaintiff's title to the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When infringement involves disputed factual questions for a jury, equity will avoid resolving them on affidavits and will send the issue to law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of hardships and irreparable harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Another element is the effect of the injunction on the defendant's business: where irreparable mischief would ensue to the defendant, it ought not to be granted, provided the plaintiff would not be injured by the delay or could be fully protected by an account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The object of the injunction is to prevent mischief but the court must preserve to each party the benefit to which he is entitled; when defendant's harm is severe and plaintiff's interests can be protected by other measures, injunction may be denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable conduct, laches, estoppel, and interim payments
rubrics_metrics.description: Nor will an injunction be granted where the plaintiff has permitted the defendant to go on and incur expense under the expectation of receiving a certain sum, if relations allow defendant to dispute the patentee's right. But where defendant is estopped at law from denying validity, an injunction will be granted; if money (e.g., a year's rent) is due, the court may order it paid into court to await trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider equitable behavior: laches, misleading conduct, or allowing defendant to make investments weigh against injunction; estoppel in favor of patentee supports it; interim equitable measures (accounts, monies into court) are available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior infringement and promises not to repeat
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plaintiff shows necessary possession and an infringement has actually been committed by the defendant, the injunction will be granted, notwithstanding the defendant admits the infringement and promises not to repeat it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere promise by a defendant not to infringe again is not a substitute for injunctive relief once the wrongful act has occurred; equity will enjoin despite such admissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final hearing expectations and consequences of delay
rubrics_metrics.description: At the final hearing the object is a perpetual injunction and objections to validity require different consideration; if the plaintiff neglected to seek interlocutory relief during the progress of the cause without satisfactory reason, the court will be disinclined to grant relief at the hearing and may dismiss the bill with costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plaintiff coming to a hearing must have his case in a state to enable adjudication; neglect or inaction during lengthy pendency can justify refusal of equitable assistance and dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies when injunction not granted simpliciter
rubrics_metrics.description: If an injunction is not to be granted simpliciter, the court can either send the plaintiff to try his title at law without an injunction, or grant an injunction but require the plaintiff to establish the patent at law; the plaintiff will be sent to law where he does not show long possession/exercise, where the injunction is resisted by evidence casting doubt on originality or infringement, or where the patent contains gross and obvious defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court tailors relief: interlocutory injunction withheld and action at law ordered where prima facie evidence is insufficient; or injunction granted subject to the patentee subsequently establishing legal title in a law action.

rubrics_metrics.name: No fixed time standard — sufficiency of elapsed time
rubrics_metrics.description: No specific lapse of time has been adopted as a standard; the general principle is that the time elapsed between granting the patent and the application for an injunction must have been sufficient to permit articles or machines to be constructed by the patentee in conformity with his claim and to be sold publicly and repeatedly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look to practical sufficiency: whether enough time has passed to allow public manufacture and sale under the patent so that enjoyment/possession evidence is meaningful; specific durations vary by case (examples range from one year to many years).
